title: The Crown of Peeled Stone
summary: A ridiculous experiment undermines an imperial coronation and helps displaced households identify their true refuge.
history: In 846, Commander Darr declared himself emperor of the chalk shelves and borrowed heavily to furnish a coronation cistern. His experimenter discovered that repeatedly peeling a dark stone produced sheets sensitive to wet fingerprints. Darr used the sheets to stage an assembly approving his annexation of neighboring terraces. Armed attendants controlled admission, and absent households were counted as consenting. After his fall in 871, the court identified a picturesque fortress as the rebels’ last refuge. Workmen later found the real shelter beneath a humble plaster yard, where fingerprints preserved evidence of people excluded from the imperial vote. The discovery endangered both victorious families and the fallen ruler’s heirs.
question: whether authenticated exclusion can revise ownership without depriving present residents of the cisterns they maintain.
transformations: An extravagant self-coronation and later rehabilitation inform a ruler whose public spectacle conceals borrowed wealth.
Playful experimentation leading to consequential material discovery becomes hand-peeling a naturally layered stone; no modern physics apparatus is imported.
A last refuge confused with a more impressive ruin becomes a dispute over which abandoned site actually sheltered the defeated.
An annexation presented as popular consent becomes a controlled terrace assembly whose exclusions survive in material evidence.
rows: Darr of the Borrowed Crown

Darr pledged five harvests of cistern fees to buy ceremonial bronze. His successors condemn his vanity while collecting the same pledged fees. A damaged household account shows that his own servants received no water during the coronation week.
The Plaster Yard Refuge

The refuge contains low benches, repaired cups, and a drain widened for many occupants. Its unheroic appearance delayed recognition. Present plaster workers fear that declaring it a sacred site will evict them from the workshops that preserved its roof.
The Peeling Table

Experimenters at the Peeling Table separate stone with resin-coated linen, wasting most sheets. Apprentices retain failed pieces to compare damp marks. The guild wants to publish its method, but imperial claimants insist the stone’s preparation is part of a private undertaking.
The Cistern Assembly

The assembly admitted terrace heads but barred households renting rooms below street level. Guards impressed absent names with borrowed signets. The surviving stone registers both official stamps and workers’ fingerprints, providing incompatible accounts of what the ceremony represented.
The Thin Crown Sheet

A sheet wrapped around Darr’s crown retained the fingerprints of its preparers. It proves that one supposed exile remained in the capital. Her descendants prefer their heroic exile story and have offered the custodian money to classify the sheet as a forgery.
The Laughing Trial

Apprentices begin testing stone with deliberately useless questions, reducing reverence for promising results. Magistrates object to jokes about ancestral testimony. The experimenters answer that a method unable to survive laughter is too vulnerable to a patron’s desired conclusion.
The Book of Unseated Names

This roster records households counted as attending the annexation assembly although their stools were empty. Its compiler also names households genuinely present under coercion. Later copies erase that distinction, simplifying resistance at the cost of the frightened people who stayed.
The Chalk Cistern Newt

Pale newts thrive in leaking refuge drains and disappear when ceremonial washing salts the water. Their absence helped identify a blocked channel. Courts interpreted it as judgment against Darr, while keepers insist the animals are responding to ruined habitat.
The Low Stair Passage

A cramped stair connected the plaster yard to an unguarded cistern. Refugees passed water skins hand to hand because adults could not turn inside it. The present owner wants to widen the stair, risking fingerprints preserved beneath its old handrail.
The Unpressed Consent Rule

Consent cannot be inferred from a blank stone panel under this ruling. Applicants must identify a living witness or documented undertaking. Counting houses resist its extension to ordinary debt rolls, where unexplained blanks have long favored the creditor.
Nessa the Sheet Keeper

Nessa repairs linen supports for fragile stone and refuses to classify a mark from shape alone. Her grandmother sheltered an imperial guard at the refuge. Publishing that fact has made both loyalists and rebels question her standing without disproving her work.
The False Last Fortress

An impressive fortress was celebrated as the final rebel shelter for three centuries. Its grain stores were too small for the reported population. The village beside it depends on commemorative visitors and seeks a history that acknowledges error without destroying its livelihood.
The Terrace Return Council

The council combines descendants of excluded households with current cistern workers. Some seek land restitution; others need uninterrupted water. Its meetings separate urgent repairs from claims of ownership, borrowing the kitchen witnesses’ method of recording actual provision before announcing benevolence.
The Second Coronation Funeral

At Darr’s funeral, creditors displayed the crown beside their unpaid tallies. Mourners removed the tallies to preserve dignity, then accidentally authenticated a revised succession account. The original debt survived in servants’ ration books discovered beneath a bier support.
The Bronze Water Seat

Darr’s ceremonial seat was hollow to reduce its cost. A seam leaks during public washing, exposing the economy beneath its imperial image. Conservators propose repairing it; creditors prefer the leak as evidence, while water carriers would rather sell the bronze for pipes.
The Empty Stool Vigil

Descendants place stools outside the annexed cistern each spring. Some newcomers participate despite having no excluded ancestor. Traditional custodians call them impostors; younger organizers argue that recognizing an exclusion does not require inheriting it.
The Refuges Compared

A mason’s manuscript compares the celebrated fortress with the plaster yard through roof capacity, drain wear, and cooking residue. Its sober measurements dismantle a popular epic. The mason deliberately includes useful evidence supplied by villagers who initially opposed his conclusion.
The Fingerprint Seep

Wet stone occasionally darkens around an old fingerprint after a household claim is denied. Comparable tests also show darkening from salt and warmth. Nessa records both conditions, preventing interpreters from presenting every stain as a dead claimant’s unambiguous demand.
Linen for Stone

Making supports for peeled sheets gives widowed spinners a new market. Dealers try to secure perpetual prices through ancestral contracts. The spinners offer seasonal commitments instead, since the amount of usable stone changes with every quarry seam.
The Refuge Compensation Hearing

Excluded heirs propose taking the false fortress’s toll income. Its residents never controlled the original annexation. The hearing must distinguish compensation for a documented wrong from punishment of a community whose inherited story was wrong.
